arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Pung's lawyer welcomed the county's concession that a taking occurred, narrowing the dispute to how much compensation is owed.
Chief Justice Roberts asked whether a fair open-market sale is the proper way to determine the property's value.
Justice Kagan observed that the county's lawyer appeared to agree foreclosure sales generally do not yield fair market prices.
Justice Alito asked whether the homeowner could have borrowed against the home's equity to pay the taxes and avoid the sale.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Isabella County foreclosed on Kevin Pung's home for unpaid taxes. The county sold the property and kept all the proceeds. Pung says the county took his home and must pay its full market value. The county says he is owed only the surplus left after his tax debt.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: A Michigan court allowed the foreclosure. The county sold the home and kept the proceeds. Pung appealed, and the Sixth Circuit ruled against him. The Supreme Court agreed to hear the case.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Pung argues the county took his home, so the Constitution requires paying its full market value, not just the leftover money.
Isabella County argues a fair foreclosure sale settles the debt, so the homeowner is entitled only to the surplus proceeds.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Pung's lawyer says history supports paying full market value when a home sells for more than the debt owed.
The county's lawyer says a fair sale process satisfies the Constitution, and the surplus is the just payment.
